# Mission

This is the brief for the project, written down from a conversation with the
owner. It is background for every worker: what we are trying to learn, why it
matters to us, and how we would like the work to feel.

## What we want

We want to understand a small system well enough to describe it in our own
words. The goal is not to build a product. It is to read widely, take notes,
and come back with a clear picture of what is known, what is guessed, and what
nobody has tried yet. A good outcome is a short set of notes that a newcomer
could read over a cup of coffee and come away with the main ideas.

We care more about honesty than about volume. If a source is weak, say so. If
two sources disagree, keep both and explain the difference. If something is
simply unknown, write that it is unknown rather than filling the gap.

## Who reads this

The owner reads everything, usually in the evening, and likes plain language.
Long paragraphs are fine when they are clear. Bullet lists are fine when they
are short. Headings should say what the section is about, not be clever.

Other workers read these notes too. They pick up where someone else left off,
so each note should stand on its own: say what it covers, where the sources
are, and what is still open.

## Topics

1. The history of the field and the people who shaped it.
2. The main ideas, in plain words, with one example each.
3. The open questions, and who is working on them now.
4. The tools people use, and what each is good and bad at.
5. The vocabulary: a short glossary of the terms that come up most.
6. Reading list: the ten things to read first, in order, with one line each.

## How we work

Work in small steps and write as you go. Notes go in the research folder, one
file per topic. Each file starts with a one-paragraph summary and ends with
its sources. Keep quotes short and always say where they came from.

Ask when something is unclear rather than guessing. It is fine to say a topic
turned out to be less interesting than expected; that is a result too.

## Tone

Friendly, direct and modest. Avoid hype. Prefer "this suggests" over "this
proves" unless it really does. Write the way you would explain it to a curious
friend who is not in the field.

## Schedule

There is no hard deadline. A first pass over every topic is more useful than a
perfect pass over one. After the first pass, we will pick the two or three
topics worth going deeper on and plan the next step together.

## Notes from the owner

- Keep it simple.
- Say what you are unsure of.
- Short is good.
- Pictures help when they explain something words do not.
- Thank you for reading this far.
